meta.case_name: Tulsa Hotel - OK or not OK?

prompt.context: Our client is a major hotel chain. They are considering acquiring an existing hotel in Tulsa, OK for $20M and expect an ROI of 20% over three years.
prompt.question: Should our client make the investment?

clarifying_info.q: How many guests per room should we assume?
clarifying_info.a: Assume single occupancy — only one guest per room.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a discounted rate for groups?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. If several rooms are reserved at once (for a group traveling together), a discounted group rate is given to each group member.

clarifying_info.q: How many operating days per year should we use?
clarifying_info.a: Assume 50 weeks per year, or 350 days per year. Round yearly profits to the nearest million.

clarifying_info.q: Should we account for seasonality or demand growth?
clarifying_info.a: Assume no seasonality in demand and no growth. Ignore time value of money.

framework: Revenue drivers: room price (individual vs. group rate) and volume (occupancy rate); also other revenue streams such as restaurant, events
Cost drivers: variable costs per occupied room and fixed costs per night
Investment analysis: compare 3-year cumulative profit to required return (20% ROI on $20M investment)
Additional factors: economic/industry trends, competitor response, client-specific synergies, risks

questions.prompt: Question 1: Should the client make the $20M acquisition given a required 20% ROI over three years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive total rooms from weekend occupancy data, then calculate weekend and weekday profits separately, sum to annual profit, and compare three-year cumulative profit to the ROI threshold. Strong candidates note that $33M >> $12M required, so invest. Bonus: mention that if an alternative project has higher ROI, it should be prioritized.

math.setup: Step 1 — derive hotel size. Weekend: 600 town visitors * 50% stay at hotel = 300 weekend guests. Weekend occupancy = 60%, so total rooms = 300 / 0.60 = 500 rooms. Step 2 — weekend day profit. Individuals: 300 * 75% * $150 = $33,750. Groups: 300 * 25% * $120 = $9,000. Variable costs: 300 * $30 = $9,000. Fixed costs: $5,750. Profit per weekend day = $33,750 + $9,000 - $9,000 - $5,750 = $28,000. Step 3 — weekday profit. Weekday guests: 500 * 75% = 375. Individuals: 375 * 40% * $150 = $22,500. Groups: 375 * 60% * $120 = $27,000. Variable costs: 375 * $30 = $11,250. Fixed costs: $5,750. Profit per weekday = $22,500 + $27,000 - $11,250 - $5,750 = $32,500. Step 4 — annual profit. Profit per week = 2 * $28,000 + 5 * $32,500 = $56,000 + $162,500 = $218,500. Annual profit = 50 * $218,500 = $10,925,000 ≈ $11M. Step 5 — 3-year profit and ROI check. 3-year profit = 3 * $11M = $33M. Required return: 20% ROI on $20M = $4M profit; total needed = $20M + $4M = $24M? (Note: casebook frames it as needing $12M in profit over 3 years to yield 20% ROI on $20M.) $33M > $12M, so the client should invest.
steps: 3-year profit: $33M; required profit for 20% ROI on $20M = $12M; $33M > $12M → invest
math.answer: Annual profit ≈ $11M; 3-year profit ≈ $33M, which exceeds the $12M required for 20% ROI. The client should make the acquisition.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Using new data (disregard Question 1 numbers) — weekend: 100 group rooms at $100, 300 individual rooms at $150; weekday: 200 group rooms at $100, 200 individual rooms at $150; 500 total rooms; variable cost $30/room/night — what is the average revenue per customer per day across the full week? Round to the nearest $10.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute a weighted average for weekend days, then weekday, then blend across a 7-day week (2 weekend days, 5 weekdays). Final answer rounds to $130.

math.setup: Average revenue per room, not net of variable cost. Compute per day type, then blend over 7 days.
math.answer: Average revenue per room per night across the week ≈ $130

questions.prompt: Question 3a (Brainstorm): What are ways the client could increase revenues at the hotel? (Assume costs are held constant.)
questions.guidance: Push candidate to generate as many structured ideas as possible across multiple categories.

questions.prompt: Question 3b (Breakeven): The client is considering a 3-year advertising campaign costing $1.5M. Using Question 2 data (average revenue $130/room/night, variable cost $30/room/night), ignore fixed costs. How many additional guests per night must the campaign attract for the client to break even? Should they launch it?
questions.guidance: Candidate should annualize campaign cost, compute contribution margin per room, derive additional guests per year, then convert to per-night. Conclude that 15 additional guests per night is very reasonable given 400 current nightly guests and 500-room capacity.

math.setup: Campaign cost spread over 3 years. Contribution margin = average revenue minus variable cost from Question 2. Solve for additional guests/year, then per night.
steps: Current occupancy is 400 rooms/night out of 500; 15 additional is a very small increment → launch the campaign
math.answer: ~15 additional guests per night; campaign should be launched.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways our client could increase revenues at the hotel? (Assume costs are held constant.)

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Raise individual room rates, positioning the hotel as a luxury destination
Implement dynamic pricing to capture higher WTP during peak periods

categories.name: Volume — Groups
ideas: Partner with a local convention center to attract large group bookings
Build or lease an on-site conference center
Contract with travel agencies or corporate travel managers

categories.name: Volume — Events
ideas: Host wedding receptions and social gatherings
Attract sports teams, academic conferences, or government delegations

categories.name: Marketing & Distribution
ideas: Run an advertising campaign online, on TV, or with travel agencies
Improve presence on hotel booking platforms (OTAs)
Leverage parent chain's loyalty program to drive bookings

categories.name: Ancillary Revenue
ideas: Open or expand a restaurant in the hotel
Add a spa, fitness center, or business center
Offer parking, room upgrades, or in-room premium services

categories.name: Capacity Expansion
ideas: Expand the hotel to add more rooms
Convert underutilized space into revenue-generating amenities

recommendation: Our client should acquire the hotel: projected 3-year profit of $33M far exceeds the $12M required to achieve a 20% ROI on the $20M investment, leaving $21M of cushion.
The client should also launch the $1.5M advertising campaign, as it requires only ~15 additional guests per night to break even — a modest increase given current occupancy of 400 out of 500 rooms.
Additional revenue levers such as partnering with a conference center or contracting with travel agencies should be explored.
Bonus: if an alternative investment offers an even higher ROI, it should be prioritized over this acquisition.
risks: National or global economic downturn could reduce business travel and tourism
Unfavorable local economic conditions in Tulsa (e.g., businesses leaving, higher local taxes) could reduce visitor traffic
A competitor could build a large hotel in Tulsa, compressing occupancy or pricing
Government could impose new taxes on hotel profits, reducing realized ROI
Actual demand may come in below projections, eroding the profit cushion
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on the specific hotel property and its current condition
Validate demand assumptions with local market data
Assess synergies with other hotels in the client's chain (brand, procurement, management systems)
Evaluate alternative investment opportunities to confirm this is the best use of $20M
